source: If I had been astonished at first catching a glimpse of so outlandish an individual as Queequeg circulating among the polite society of a civilized town, that astonishment soon departed upon taking my first daylight stroll through the streets of New Bedford.

In thoroughfares nigh the docks, any considerable seaport will frequently offer to view the queerest looking nondescripts from foreign parts. Even in Broadway and Chestnut streets, Mediterranean mariners will sometimes jostle the affrighted ladies. Regent Street is not unknown to Lascars and Malays; and at Bombay, in the Apollo Green, live Yankees have often scared the natives. But New Bedford beats all Water Street and Wapping. In these last-mentioned haunts you see only sailors; but in New Bedford, actual cannibals stand chatting at street corners; savages outright; many of whom yet carry on their bones unholy flesh. It makes a stranger stare.

But, besides the Feegeeans, Tongatobooarrs, Erromanggoans, Pannangians, and Brighggians, and, besides the wild specimens of the whaling-craft which unheeded reel about the streets, you will see other sights still more curious, certainly more comical. There weekly arrive in this town scores of green Vermonters and New Hampshire men, all athirst for gain and glory in the fishery. They are mostly young, of stalwart frames; fellows who have felled forests, and now seek to drop the axe and snatch the whale-lance. Many are as green as the Green Mountains whence they came. In some things you would think them but a few hours old. Look there! that chap strutting round the corner. He wears a beaver hat and swallow-tailed coat, girdled with a sailor-belt and sheath-knife. Here comes another with a sou’-wester and a bombazine cloak.

No town-bred dandy will compare with a country-bred one—I mean a downright bumpkin dandy—a fellow that, in the dog-days, will mow his two acres in buckskin gloves for fear of tanning his hands. Now when a country dandy like this takes it into his head to make a distinguished reputation, and joins the great whale-fishery, you should see the comical things he does upon reaching the seaport. In bespeaking his sea-outfit, he orders bell-buttons to his waistcoats; straps to his canvas trowsers. Ah, poor Hay-Seed! how bitterly will burst those straps in the first howling gale, when thou art driven, straps, buttons, and all, down the throat of the tempest.

But think not that this famous town has only harpooneers, cannibals, and bumpkins to show her visitors. Not at all. Still New Bedford is a queer place. Had it not been for us whalemen, that tract of land would this day perhaps have been in as howling condition as the coast of Labrador. As it is, parts of her back country are enough to frighten one, they look so bony. The town itself is perhaps the dearest place to live in, in all New England. It is a land of oil, true enough: but not like Canaan; a land, also, of corn and wine. The streets do not run with milk; nor in the spring-time do they pave them with fresh eggs. Yet, in spite of this, nowhere in all America will you find more patrician-like houses; parks and gardens more opulent, than in New Bedford. Whence came they? how planted upon this once scraggy scoria of a country?

Go and gaze upon the iron emblematical harpoons round yonder lofty mansion, and your question will be answered. Yes; all these brave houses and flowery gardens came from the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans. One and all, they were harpooned and dragged up hither from the bottom of the sea. Can Herr Alexander perform a feat like that?

In New Bedford, fathers, they say, give whales for dowers to their daughters, and portion off their nieces with a few porpoises a-piece. You must go to New Bedford to see a brilliant wedding; for, they say, they have reservoirs of oil in every house, and every night recklessly burn their lengths in spermaceti candles.

In summer time, the town is sweet to see; full of fine maples—long avenues of green and gold. And in August, high in air, the beautiful and bountiful horse-chestnuts, candelabra-wise, proffer the passer-by their tapering upright cones of congregated blossoms. So omnipotent is art; which in many a district of New Bedford has superinduced bright terraces of flowers upon the barren refuse rocks thrown aside at creation’s final day.

And the women of New Bedford, they bloom like their own red roses. But roses only bloom in summer; whereas the fine carnation of their cheeks is perennial as sunlight in the seventh heavens. Elsewhere match that bloom of theirs, ye cannot, save in Salem, where they tell me the young girls breathe such musk, their sailor sweethearts smell them miles off shore, as though they were drawing nigh the odorous Moluccas instead of the Puritanic sands.

modern_en.title: Chapter 6 — The Street
paragraphs: If I'd been astonished at first seeing someone as outlandish as Queequeg strolling through the polite society of a civilized town, my surprise quickly vanished during my first daylight walk through New Bedford's streets.

In the streets near the docks, any sizable seaport will often put on view the strangest-looking nondescripts from foreign parts. Even on Broadway and Chestnut Street, Mediterranean sailors will sometimes jostle the frightened ladies. Regent Street is no stranger to Lascars and Malays; and at Bombay, on the Apollo Green, live Yankees have often scared the natives. But New Bedford beats every Water Street and Wapping. In those last-mentioned haunts you see only sailors; but in New Bedford, actual cannibals stand chatting on street corners — savages outright, many of whom still carry unholy flesh on their bones. It makes a stranger stare.

But besides the Fijians, Tongatobooarrs, Erromanggoans, Pannangians, and Brighggians, and besides the wild specimens of the whaling trade who reel unnoticed about the streets, you will see other sights still more curious, and certainly more comical. Every week scores of green Vermonters and New Hampshire men arrive in this town, all thirsting for gain and glory in the fishery. They are mostly young, with stalwart frames — fellows who have felled forests and now want to drop the axe and snatch up the whale-lance. Many are as green as the Green Mountains they came from. In some things you would think them only a few hours old. Look there! That fellow strutting around the corner. He wears a beaver hat and a swallow-tailed coat, belted with a sailor's belt and sheath-knife. Here comes another in a sou'wester and a bombazine cloak.

No town-bred dandy can compare with a country-bred one — I mean a downright bumpkin dandy, a fellow who in the dog-days of summer will mow his two acres in buckskin gloves for fear of tanning his hands. Now when a country dandy like this takes it into his head to make himself a distinguished reputation, and joins the great whale fishery, you should see the comical things he does when he reaches the seaport. Ordering his sea outfit, he has bell-buttons put on his waistcoats and straps on his canvas trousers. Ah, poor Hay-Seed! How bitterly those straps will burst in the first howling gale, when you are driven, straps, buttons, and all, down the throat of the tempest.

But don't think that this famous town has only harpooners, cannibals, and bumpkins to show its visitors. Not at all. Still, New Bedford is a strange place. If it hadn't been for us whalemen, that tract of land might to this day be in as howling a condition as the coast of Labrador. As it is, parts of its back country are enough to frighten you, they look so bony. The town itself is perhaps the most expensive place to live in all New England. It is a land of oil, true enough — but not like Canaan, a land also of corn and wine. The streets do not run with milk; nor in springtime do they pave them with fresh eggs. Yet in spite of this, nowhere in all America will you find more patrician-looking houses, or more opulent parks and gardens, than in New Bedford. Where did they come from? How were they planted on this once scraggy cinder-heap of a country?

Go and gaze at the iron harpoons set as emblems around that lofty mansion over there, and your question will be answered. Yes; all these fine houses and flowery gardens came from the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans. One and all, they were harpooned and dragged up here from the bottom of the sea. Can Herr Alexander, the stage conjurer, perform a trick like that?

In New Bedford, they say, fathers give whales to their daughters as dowries, and portion off their nieces with a few porpoises apiece. You must go to New Bedford to see a brilliant wedding; for, they say, they have reservoirs of oil in every house, and every night recklessly burn spermaceti candles down to their full length.

In summertime the town is sweet to see, full of fine maples — long avenues of green and gold. And in August, high in the air, the beautiful and bountiful horse-chestnuts, like candelabra, offer the passer-by their tapering upright cones of clustered blossoms. So all-powerful is art, which in many a district of New Bedford has laid bright terraces of flowers over the barren refuse rocks thrown aside on creation's final day.

And the women of New Bedford bloom like their own red roses. But roses bloom only in summer; the fine carnation of their cheeks is perennial as sunlight in the seventh heaven. Nowhere else can you match that bloom — except in Salem, where they say the young girls breathe such musk that their sailor sweethearts can smell them miles offshore, as if they were approaching the fragrant Moluccas instead of the Puritan sands.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 6 — Gaden
paragraphs: Hvis jeg var blevet forbavset over at se en så sælsom skikkelse som Queequeg spadsere rundt i en civiliseret bys fine selskab, forsvandt min forbavselse hurtigt under min første gåtur i dagslys gennem New Bedfords gader.

I gaderne nær dokkerne vil enhver stor havneby ofte vise de mærkeligst udseende ubestemmelige skikkelser fra fremmede egne. Selv på Broadway og Chestnut Street skubber middelhavssømænd nogle gange til de forskrækkede damer. Regent Street kender godt til lascarer og malajer, og i Bombay, på Apollo Green, har levende yankeer ofte skræmt de indfødte. Men New Bedford slår enhver Water Street og Wapping. På de sidstnævnte steder ser man kun sømænd, men i New Bedford står egentlige kannibaler og sludrer på gadehjørnerne — vilde helt igennem, hvoraf mange stadig bærer uhelligt kød på knoglerne. Det får en fremmed til at måbe.

Men udover fijianerne, Tongatobooarrerne, Erromanggoanerne, Pannangianerne og Brighggianerne og udover de vilde eksemplarer af hvalfangerfaget, som vakler upåagtet rundt i gaderne, kan man se andre syn, der er endnu mærkeligere og bestemt mere komiske. Hver uge ankommer snesevis af grønne vermontere og mænd fra New Hampshire til denne by, alle sultne efter vinding og ære i fiskeriet. De er for det meste unge og kraftigt byggede — karle, der har fældet skove og nu vil lægge øksen og gribe hvallansen. Mange er lige så grønne som de Green Mountains, de kommer fra. På nogle områder skulle man tro, at de kun var få timer gamle. Se dér! Den fyr, der stolterer om hjørnet. Han har bæverhat og frakke med svalehaler på, spændt med et sømandsbælte og en skedekniv. Her kommer en anden i sydvest og bombasinkappe.

Ingen bydandy kan måle sig med en landdandy — jeg mener en gennemført bondeknold af en dandy, en fyr, som i sommerens hundedage vil slå sine to acres med hjorteskindshandsker på af frygt for at blive solbrændt på hænderne. Når nu sådan en landdandy får det i hovedet, at han vil skabe sig et fornemt navn, og melder sig til det store hvalfiskeri, skulle man se de komiske ting, han gør, når han når frem til havnebyen. Han bestiller sit søtøj og får klokkeknapper sat på sine veste og stropper på sine lærredsbukser. Ak, stakkels Hø-Frø! Hvor bittert vil disse stropper sprænges i den første hylende storm, når du bliver jaget, stropper, knapper og alt, ned i stormens strube.

Men tro ikke, at denne berømte by kun har harpunerere, kannibaler og bønderknolde at byde de besøgende på. Slet ikke. New Bedford er alligevel et besynderligt sted. Hvis ikke det havde været for os hvalfangere, kunne dette stykke land den dag i dag have været lige så øde og stormomsust som kysten af Labrador. Som det er, er dele af baglandet nok til at skræmme én, så nøgent og benet ser det ud. Selve byen er måske det dyreste sted at bo i hele New England. Det er et landskab fuldt af olie, det er sandt nok — men ikke som Kanaan, der også var et land med korn og vin. Gaderne flyder ikke med mælk, og om foråret brolægger man dem ikke med friske æg. Alligevel finder man ingen steder i hele Amerika flere fornemme huse eller mere overdådige parker og haver end i New Bedford. Hvor kom de fra? Hvordan blev de plantet på dette engang så magre og forblæste askedynge af et land?

Gå hen og se på de jernharpuner, der sidder som emblemer rundt om det høje palæ derovre, så får du svar. Ja, alle disse fine huse og blomstrende haver kommer fra Atlanterhavet, Stillehavet og Det Indiske Ocean. Hver eneste en af dem blev harpuneret og slæbt herop fra havets bund. Kan Herr Alexander, scenetrylleren, udføre sådan et kunststykke?

I New Bedford siger man, at fædrene giver deres døtre hvaler i medgift og udstyrer deres niecer med et par marsvin hver. Man må rejse til New Bedford for at se et brillant bryllup. For man siger, at de har oliebeholdere i hvert eneste hus og hver aften hensynsløst brænder spermacetlys helt ned til stumpen.

Om sommeren er byen smuk at se på, fuld af flotte ahorntræer — lange alléer i grønt og guld. Og i august rækker de skønne, rigt blomstrende hestekastanjer højt op i luften og byder den forbipasserende deres smalle, oprejste kogler af tætte blomster, ligesom kandelabre. Så almægtig er kunsten, der i mange af New Bedfords kvarterer har lagt lyse terrasser af blomster over de golde klipper, som blev kastet til side som affald på skabelsens sidste dag.

Og kvinderne i New Bedford blomstrer som byens egne røde roser. Men roser blomstrer kun om sommeren, mens den fine nellikerøde farve på deres kinder varer ved som sollyset i den syvende himmel. Ingen andre steder kan man finde en sådan blomstring — undtagen i Salem, hvor man siger, at de unge piger ånder så meget moskusduft ud, at deres sømandskærester kan lugte dem mange engelske mil fra land, som om de var på vej mod de duftende Moluk-øer og ikke mod puritanernes sand.
